questions.q:
Nearly a third of Delhi’s garbage goes untreated every day and leaches into the environment, an independent audit has found. This is to say that of the roughly 11,000 tonnes of waste that the Capital churns out every day, at least 3,500 tonnes is allowed to go unprocessed, only to end up further swelling the city’s gargantuan garbage mountains. Tackling this has been Delhi’s biggest civic challenge for years, one that it has responded to feebly, but also one that will only get more acute with time. Indeed, Delhi is not the only megapolis that has struggled to rein in its solid waste problem. Burgeoning populations, increasing urbanisation and soaring consumption mean cities will continue spitting out more waste. Municipal authorities need to take note of these shifts and design effective strategies to keep this waste from roiling the environment.
To this effect, the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD)’s audit is a good first step that acknowledges the scale of the problem. But the civic body now needs to effect a series of measures that will need to work in lockstep to dial down the volume of untreated waste. In the short term, it will need a robust doorstep waste collection mechanism, to ensure effective segregation of wet and dry waste, shore up the waste management system, and improve monitoring. Over the long term, the civic body must promote new recycling techniques and cut leakages, while also improving efficiency at the city’s collection points. This will require the MCD to harness technology, including best practices from other parts of the world, and engage the citizenry, educating them on waste management while persuading them to collaborate with public agencies in collection, recycling and disposal.
What is the tone of the passage discussing waste management in Delhi?
questions.solution:
C) Critical
The tone of the passage is critical, evident from how it highlights the significant challenge of managing waste in Delhi, where a substantial portion of garbage goes untreated every day. The passage critically assesses the efforts made by the city's authorities, noting them as "feebly" responsive to the escalating problem. It underscores the urgency and the inadequacy of the current measures, indicating a critical viewpoint towards the management of waste and the need for more effective strategies.

Addressing the soaring consumption rates that lead directly to increased production of waste, specifically electronic waste.
Tackling the problem of untreated garbage, which contributes to the swelling of the city's garbage mountains and poses a significant environmental threat.
questions.solution:
D) Tackling the problem of untreated garbage, which contributes to the swelling of the city's garbage mountains and poses a significant environmental threat.
The passage explicitly identifies the management of untreated garbage as Delhi's biggest civic challenge. It mentions that a significant portion of the daily waste goes untreated, contributing to the growing garbage mountains in the city. This issue has been a long-standing challenge for Delhi, one that has been met with feeble responses and is expected to become more acute over time. The other options, while they may represent valid urban challenges, are not mentioned in the passage as the primary issue facing Delhi.

questions.q:
Nearly a third of Delhi’s garbage goes untreated every day and leaches into the environment, an independent audit has found. This is to say that of the roughly 11,000 tonnes of waste that the Capital churns out every day, at least 3,500 tonnes is allowed to go unprocessed, only to end up further swelling the city’s gargantuan garbage mountains. Tackling this has been Delhi’s biggest civic challenge for years, one that it has responded to feebly, but also one that will only get more acute with time. Indeed, Delhi is not the only megapolis that has struggled to rein in its solid waste problem. Burgeoning populations, increasing urbanisation and soaring consumption mean cities will continue spitting out more waste. Municipal authorities need to take note of these shifts and design effective strategies to keep this waste from roiling the environment.
To this effect, the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD)’s audit is a good first step that acknowledges the scale of the problem. But the civic body now needs to effect a series of measures that will need to work in lockstep to dial down the volume of untreated waste. In the short term, it will need a robust doorstep waste collection mechanism, to ensure effective segregation of wet and dry waste, shore up the waste management system, and improve monitoring. Over the long term, the civic body must promote new recycling techniques and cut leakages, while also improving efficiency at the city’s collection points. This will require the MCD to harness technology, including best practices from other parts of the world, and engage the citizenry, educating them on waste management while persuading them to collaborate with public agencies in collection, recycling and disposal.
For long-term waste management improvement, what is one of the strategies the MCD must focus on according to the passage?
options: Phasing out public participation in waste management
Reducing the emphasis on recycling to focus on incineration
Promoting new recycling techniques and improving efficiency
Completely outsourcing waste management to private entities
questions.solution:
C) Promoting new recycling techniques and improving efficiency
The passage outlines that, over the long term, the MCD needs to "promote new recycling techniques and cut leakages, while also improving efficiency at the city’s collection points." This approach indicates a multi-faceted strategy involving technological advancement in recycling and operational improvements.
